Lust (rāga) is the near enemy of loving-kindness, being like it in seeing virtues; it finds an opening quickly, so loving-kindness must be well guarded from it; ill will (vyāpāda) is the far enemy, like a man's enemy who lives hidden in mountain thickets, alike by being unlike, so one develops loving-kindness fearlessly from it; it is impossible for one who has loving-kindness to be angry.
Missing what one had can look like compassion, the text says, because both see what has gone wrong. It keeps the two apart.

3. What the text says, read closely: The good (śreyas) is one thing, the pleasant (preyas) another; both bind a person with different aims. Good comes to one who takes the good; one who chooses the pleasant misses the goal. Both come to a person; the wise one examines and distinguishes them; the wise prefers the good to the pleasant; the fool chooses the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping (yogakṣema).
